extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, history, and American democratic institutions (general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century political and social analysis of the present and probable future condition of the three races (whites, negroes, and Indians) inhabiting the territory of the United States, focusing on causes of decline, assimilation, and power relations. The text offers causal claims and predictions about survival, assimilation, and social consequences of institutions and customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two alternatives for Indian survival: war or civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indians had only the two alternatives of war or civilization; in other words, they must either have destroyed the Europeans or become their equals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a decisive dichotomy/predictor of the native population's fate: without the capacity to unite and expel Europeans (war) or to assimilate and become social equals (civilization), extinction is the likely outcome. The text uses this as a criterion for predicting disappearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilization requires fixation and agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilization is the result of a long social process which takes place in the same spot, and is handed down from one generation to another... it is first necessary to fix it; which cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil; the Indians ought in the first place to have been accustomed to agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful 'civilization' (i.e., sustained integration into settled, agricultural, intergenerational society) requires sedentism and transmission of social practices; attempts to educate nomadic/hunter peoples without settling them are predicted to fail. Use this as a standard for evaluating likelihood of assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobility/dancer-of-the-chase undermines civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all nations, those submit to civilization with the most difficulty which habitually live by the chase... the dwelling of the hunter varies with that of the animals he pursues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomadic/hunting lifeways are highlighted as intrinsically incompatible with the slow, place-based processes that produce settled civilization; persistence of migratory habits is an indicator that attempts at permanent social change will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: European trade goods and technologies increase Indian wants while reducing their resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The Europeans introduced amongst the savages... fire-arms, ardent spirits, and iron: they taught them to exchange for manufactured stuffs the rough garments which had previously satisfied their untutored simplicity... whilst the wants of the natives were thus increasing, their resources continued to diminish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction of European goods creates dependency: new wants that require goods the Indians cannot produce, while European settlement and hunting drive game away. This dynamic is used as a causal mechanism explaining displacement and decline; assess presence of such trade/technology dependencies as predictors of dispossession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famine/game displacement is the practical driver of Indian retreat
rubrics_metrics.description: To drive away their game is to deprive them of the means of existence... it is not the Europeans who drive away the native inhabitants of America; it is famine which compels them to recede.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames ecological/economic pressure (loss of game) as the proximate cause forcing tribes to vacate lands. Evaluate settlement impact on resources (game, buffalo) as a metric for likelihood of forced migration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forced treaties and manipulative bargaining produce dispossession
rubrics_metrics.description: The government... assemble the Indians... display before the eyes of the Indians firearms, woollen garments, kegs of brandy... If, when they have beheld all these riches, they still hesitate, it is insinuated that they have not the means of refusing... Half convinced, and half compelled, they go to inhabit new deserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice of treaty-ground bargaining with displays of goods, inducements to immediate consumption, and implicit coercion is identified as a procedural mechanism by which large territorial cessions are obtained. Treaties negotiated under these conditions are presented as a predictable path to land loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servility produced by slavery degrades negroes' capacity for freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Violence made him a slave, and the habit of servitude gives him the thoughts and desires of a slave... If he becomes free, independence is often felt by him to be a heavier burden than slavery... while servitude brutalizes, liberty destroys him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats long-term slavery as producing psychological and social dispositions (admiration of masters, lack of experience in self-governance) that make the transition to liberty dangerous or destructive. This is used as an evaluative claim about the negro population's prospects under emancipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian pride/resistance causes rejection of European assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indian... has his imagination inflated with the pretended nobility of his origin, and lives and dies in the midst of these dreams of pride... Far from desiring to conform his habits to ours, he loves his savage life as the distinguishing mark of his race, and he repels every advance to civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast to the negro: the Indian's cultural pride and attachment to his own ways makes voluntary assimilation unlikely; cultural identity and refusal to imitate Europeans are indicators that assimilation policies will have limited success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial hierarchy and lack of amalgamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Three races, naturally distinct... are discoverable amongst them... they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart... the white or European, the man pre-eminent; and in subordinate grades, the negro and the Indian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts an observed social ranking and lack of racial blending as a structural feature of American society: use presence of segregation, legal status differences, and social distance as metrics for assessing long-term social trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline of family ties and social intermediaries weakens resistance to centralized power
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as family feeling was kept alive, the antagonist of oppression was never alone... But when patrimonial estates are divided... where can family feeling be found? ... every citizen—being equally weak, equally poor, and equally dependent—has only his personal impotence to oppose to the organized force of the government?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The erosion of intermediate social structures (families, corporations, charters) is presented as a criterion by which citizens' capacity to resist tyranny is measured; the loss of social anchors predicts vulnerability to centralized authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: If democratic institutions are not gradually introduced, society faces either democratic liberty or Caesar-like tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: They will soon be left with no other alternative than democratic liberty, or the tyranny of the Caesars... if we do not succeed in gradually introducing democratic institutions... there will be no independence at all... but an equal tyranny over all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high-level predictive standard: the institutional path chosen (gradual democratization versus abrupt or absent reform) is the decisive factor determining whether equality leads to freedom or uniform despotism. Assess the pace and nature of institutional reform when forecasting political outcomes.
